problem: Find the surface area of the part of the hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that is subject to the constraints ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1$ and $y\ge 0.$
worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1,\,y\ge 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/e7cb4d16f39d1c1e38d65000471cbc5ca1831a0bbc2cfc61c4f03d087d6a5125.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=4-{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=-2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 4 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r & =-\pi {\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{4}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi \cdot 2{({u}^{1/2})}_{3}^{4} \\  & =2\pi \cdot ({4}^{1/2}-{3}^{1/2}) \\  & =2\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$
